title: A cauldron of loves (Confessions 3.1)
hookLine: young Augustine in Carthage, in love with being in love
tomorrow: when a friend dies, what does everything you look at become?
last: SIX LINES FROM THE DESERT AND A PRAYER.

lines: IN LOVE WITH BEING IN LOVE.
cards: Some playlists are all longing: songs about someone, with no someone yet. Augustine describes that from a big, loud city. Carthage, and a young man newly arrived.
Looking back years later, the first thing he remembers is noise. All around him, he says, a cauldron of unholy loves was sizzling and singing. He isn't in love with anyone yet.
He's in love with being in love.

teach.b: Here is his line, in plain English: I did not love yet, and I loved to love; I went looking for something to love, in love with loving. No villain, no scandal named. Just a hunger without an object.
Then he says what he thinks the hunger really was: a famine of inward food, and that food was God. He didn't feel hungry for that. He felt hungry for everything else.
One for a friend tonight: some readers hear a pun in the Latin, where the city is Carthago and the cauldron is sartago, a frying pan. A city that sizzles.
And the Confessions is still a prayer, spoken to God, so this isn't bragging about wild years or beating himself up.
The point isn't that love is bad; Augustine spends the rest of the book on love.
It's what yesterday's restless heart looks like from the inside.

how: Christians from different churches read Augustine's Confessions as spiritual reading, some slowly, a book at a time, and some read it as a prayer alongside their own.

games.q: what does “a cauldron of loves” mean?
o: a pot of stew cooked at a Carthage feast
a heart in love with love, in a sizzling city
a magic potion from an old love story

games.q: a cauldron of loves — tap the pairs.
p: the loud city where he arrived
what he says the hunger was for

s: in this chapter Augustine names a scandal and a villain
he names no one: just a hunger, in love with loving.
Augustine says love itself is the problem
the popular reading. he spends the rest of the book on love; the trouble is what it's for.
the Confessions is written as a prayer spoken to God
he tells his story to God, not to a crowd.

games.q: your cousin starts a new relationship the week the last one ends, and laughs, 'i just love love.' what would Augustine ask her?
o: so who's next on the list?
what are you really hungry for?
why not swear off dating for good?
games.why: Augustine read his own hunger as a famine of inward food. he didn't scold the loving; he asked what it was for.

practice: Take a pen and write one line by hand: something you're in love with right now, a person, a plan, a screen, a hope. Under it, write what hunger it might be feeding.
Don't judge either line; just look at them for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: A cauldron of loves. Augustine's picture of Carthage: a pot sizzling with loves, and a heart in love with love itself.

orig.note: Latin: I loved to love. from Confessions 3.1, nondum amabam, et amare amabam: I did not love yet, and I loved to love.

carryVoice: Your line: in love with love. A hunger still looking for its food. That's the week, done.
